An Improved Bound for Testing _k_-Colorability Bangjie Xu
Tsinghua University
`xbj24@mails.tsinghua.edu.cn` **Abstract** We study the sample complexity of testing _k_-colorability in the dense graph model. A graph is \(\varepsilon\)-far from being _k_-colorable if at least \(\varepsilon n^2\) edge deletions are required to make it _k_-colorable. We prove that a uniformly random induced subgraph on \(O(klogk/\varepsilon)\) vertices is non-_k_-colorable with probability at least 2/3 whenever the original graph is \(\varepsilon\)-far from _k_-colorable. The proof combines a palette-based coloring process with a container-style encoding-and-reconstruction argument. This yields \(O(klogk/\varepsilon)\), which is no worse than the previous state of the art \(O(klog(1/\varepsilon)/\varepsilon)\) throughout the nonvacuous parameter range, and is an improvement when \(logk=o(log(1/\varepsilon))\). For each fixed _k_, combining this upper bound with the known \(\Omega(logk/\varepsilon)\) lower bound gives \(\Theta(1/\varepsilon)\) dependence on \(\varepsilon\). ## 1 Introduction Deciding whether a graph _G_ satisfies \(\chi(G)\le k\) is NP-complete for every fixed \(k\ge 3\) [16, 15]; under the Exponential Time Hypothesis it cannot be decided in time 2_o(n_) [17], where _n_ is the number of vertices; nevertheless, extensive researches have shown that for every fixed _k_ it can be decided in exponential but sub-2_n_ time: for _k_=3 there is an algorithm running in time _O_(1.3289_n_) [10], for _k_=4 one running in time _O_(1.7159_n_) [24], and for every fixed _k_ there is \(\varepsilon_k>0\) such that _k_-colorability can be decided by a randomized algorithm in time \(O((2-\varepsilon_k)n)\) [25]. In fact, for arbitrary _k_ and _n_ there are _n_-vertex graphs of chromatic number _k_ whose induced subgraphs on linear-size vertex sets are all 3-colorable [11]. This lack of local witnesses is what makes the global condition \(\chi(G)>k\) hard to detect, and it is what makes testing _k_-colorability nontrivial. However, a body of work has shown that if there is a substantial gap between _G_ and a _k_-colorable graph (that is, a constant fraction of _G_’s edges has to be deleted before it becomes _k_-colorable), then even a random small induced subgraph of _G_ is non-_k_-colorable with constant probability, where the size of the subgraph depends only on _k_ and \(\varepsilon\) and not on |_V(G_)|. A graph _G_ on _n_ vertices is \(\varepsilon\)-far from being _k_-colorable if at least \(\varepsilon n^2\) of its edges have to be removed to make it _k_-colorable, and the sample complexity \(S_k(n,\varepsilon)\) of _k_-colorability is the smallest _q_ such that, for every \(\varepsilon\)-far _G_ with _n_ vertices, a uniformly random _q_-vertex induced subgraph of _G_ is non-_k_-colorable with probability at least 2/3. The quantity \(S_k(n,\varepsilon)\) is an important parameter in property testing in the dense graph model [13, 14, 12]; it is the minimum sample complexity of a canonical \(\varepsilon\)-tester for _k_-colorability on graphs over _n_ vertices. As we will soon see, \(S_k(n,\varepsilon)\) is in fact independent of _n_, so throughout the rest of the paper we write \(S_k(\varepsilon)\). Bollobás, Erdős, Simonovits and Szemerédi [9] showed for _k_=2, and Rödl and Duke [20] showed for every fixed _k_ the existence of a constant \(f_k(\varepsilon)\) such that any graph having sufficiently many vertices that is \(\varepsilon\)-far from being _k_-colorable has an induced subgraph with no more than \(f_k(\varepsilon)\) vertices that is non-_k_-colorable; both proofs used Szemerédi’s regularity lemma [23]. Their proofs can be reorganized to show that a random sample of \(C(\varepsilon,k)\) (which is independent of _n_) vertices

succeeds with constant probability. Goldreich, Goldwasser and Ron \[13\] abandoned regularity altogether and, by constructively extending partitions of the graph, obtained the polynomial bound \(S_k(\varepsilon)=\tilde{O}(k^2/\varepsilon^3)\) for \(k\ge 3\) and \(\tilde{O}(1/\varepsilon^2)\) for _k_=2. Alon and Krivelevich \[1\] improved the bound to \(\tilde{O}(k/\varepsilon^2)\) for \(k\ge 3\) and \(\tilde{O}(1/\varepsilon)\) for _k_=2 by growing a tree of colorings of the sample, and they also proved the lower bound \(S_k(\varepsilon)=\Omega(1/\varepsilon)\). Sohler \[22\] then obtained \(\tilde{O}(k^6/\varepsilon)\), by reducing the problem to the satisfiability of a constraint satisfaction problem.

More recently, Blais and Seth \[7, 8\] obtained \(S_k(\varepsilon)=O(\frac{k}{\varepsilon}log^2\frac{1}{\varepsilon})\) by introducing the container method of extremal combinatorics \[18, 6, 21\] into property testing. Kushnir and Shapira \[19\] refined this analysis, removing a factor of \(log(1/\varepsilon)\) and thereby attaining \(O(\frac{k}{\varepsilon}log\frac{1}{\varepsilon})\), which was the previous state of the art, and they also proved a lower bound \(S_k(\varepsilon)=\Omega(logk/\varepsilon)\), conjecturing that \(\Theta(logk/\varepsilon)\) is the truth. In this paper, we prove an upper bound of \(O(\frac{k}{\varepsilon}logk)\) (Theorem 1.1 below).

**Theorem 1.1.** _For every integer_ \(k\ge 2\) _and every_ \(\varepsilon>0\), <sup>1</sup><tbc>

\(S_k(\varepsilon)=O\big(\frac{k}{\varepsilon}logk\big),\)

<tbc>_with an absolute implied constant. More explicitly, choose_<tbc>

\(T:=\left\lceil\frac{4k}{\varepsilon}\right\rceil,\alpha:=\frac{\varepsilon}{4(k+1)},\)

<tbc>_and set_

\(q:=max\left\{4T,\left\lceil\frac{4}{\alpha}log(16k)\right\rceil\right\}.\)

_Then every n-vertex graph that is_ \(\varepsilon\)_-far from being k-colorable has a non-k-colorable induced subgraph on q uniformly sampled vertices with probability at least_ 2/3.

Comparing with the former upper bound of \(O(\frac{k}{\varepsilon}log\frac{1}{\varepsilon})\) of Kushnir and Shapira \[19\], by the conclusion of Lemma 3.2 below, the new bound is no worse than the previous one throughout the nonvacuous parameter range, since \(\varepsilon<1/(2k)\) implies \(logk<log\frac{1}{\varepsilon}\). Moreover, it is a strict improvement whenever \(1/\varepsilon\) is superpolynomial in _k_. Also, if _k_ is fixed, our upper bound matches the existing best lower bound of \(\Omega(\frac{logk}{\varepsilon})\) up to a constant factor, which shows that the sample complexity (treating _k_ as constant) is \(\Theta(\frac{1}{\varepsilon})\).

In general, a container argument compresses a large family of combinatorial objects by recording a relatively small fingerprint and associating it with a container that covers every object having that fingerprint. The counting is based on the fingerprints and the containers they correspond to. In this paper, the proof idea is a combination of containers and palettes. The use of palettes and lists of available colors is classical in graph coloring, see, for example, work on bounded-palette list coloring and palette sparsification \[3, 2, 5, 4\].

Our algorithmic mechanism is different from \[7, 19\]’s. For each original vertex, we use the minimum monochromatic degree over all colors that remain available in its palette. In our process, the deletion triggered by a degree threshold empties the entire palette of an original vertex, rather than removing a single vertex–color copy. After defining a graph consisting of _k_ copies of the original graph, \[7, 19\] introduce a container process that, in fact, applies to any undirected graph. In this paper, we restate the process from the perspective of palettes to make the proof appear more natural.

<sup>1</sup>Our proof also applies when _k_=1. Thus, a formulation valid for all integers \(k\ge 1\) is \(O(klog(k+1)/\varepsilon)\).

## 2 Notation and conventions

We work throughout with finite simple graphs. In particular, all graphs considered below are nonempty, and we write \(n:=|V(G)|\ge 1\). For an integer \(k\ge 1\), write [_k_]={1_,...,k_}. All logarithms are natural.

A graph _G_ is called \(\varepsilon\)-far from being _k_-colorable if at least \(\varepsilon n^2\) edges must be deleted from _G_ in order to obtain a _k_-colorable graph. The sample complexity \(S_k(\varepsilon)\) is the smallest positive integer _q_ with the following property: for every \(\varepsilon\)-far graph _G_, a uniformly random _q_-vertex induced subgraph is non-_k_-colorable with probability at least 2/3. If _q\>n_, we sample all vertices.

For a map \(c:V(G)\rightarrow[k]\), let _M(c_) denote the set of monochromatic edges, that is, edges _uv_ with _c(u_)=_c(v_). Thus |_M(c_)| is the number of monochromatic edges under _c_.

A palette system _P_ assigns to each vertex _v_ a set \(P(v)\subseteq[k]\), and empty palettes are allowed. Define<tbc>

\(U(P):=\{v:P(v)\neq\varnothing\}.\)

<tbc>For \(i\in P(v)\), set<tbc>

\(d_i^P(v):=|\{u\in N_G(v):i\in P(u)\}|,m_P(v):=min_{i\in P(v)}d_i^P(v).\)

<tbc>The label count of _P_ is

\(\lambda(P):=\sum_{v\in V(G)}|P(v)|.\)

We write \(P'\subseteq P\) if \(P'(v)\subseteq P(v)\) for every vertex _v_.

For positive integers _r_, let

\(P_N^r:=N(N-1)\cdots(N-r+1)\)

be the number of ordered _r_-tuples of distinct elements from an _N_-element set. We set \(P_N^r=0\) when _r\>N_.

## 3 Distance characterization

**Lemma 3.1.** _A graph G is_ \(\varepsilon\)_-far from being k-colorable if and only if every map_ \(c:V(G)\rightarrow[k]\) _satisfies_<tbc>

\(|M(c)|\ge\varepsilon n^2.\)

<tbc>_Proof._ For a fixed map _c_, deleting all monochromatic edges makes _c_ a proper _k_-coloring. Conversely, if deleting an edge set makes _c_ proper, then that edge set contains every monochromatic edge of _c_. Hence the minimum number of deletions needed to obtain a _k_-colorable graph is

\(min_{c:V(G)\rightarrow[k]}|M(c)|,\)

which proves the claim.

**Lemma 3.2.** _If there exists an n-vertex_ \(\varepsilon\)_-far graph with_ \(n\ge 1\)_, then_<tbc>

\(\varepsilon<\frac{1}{2k}.\)

_Proof._ Color every vertex independently and uniformly from \[_k_\]. Every edge is monochromatic with probability 1_/k_, and therefore<tbc>

\(\mathbb{E}|M(c)|=\frac{|E(G)|}{k}\le\frac{\genfrac(){pt}{2}{n}{2}}{k}=\frac{n(n-1)}{2k}<\frac{n^2}{2k}.\)

<tbc>Thus some map _c_<sub>0</sub> satisfies |_M(c_<sub>0</sub>)|_\<n_<sup>2</sup>/(2_k_). By Lemma 3.1, every map has at least \(\varepsilon n^2\) monochromatic edges. Hence

\(\varepsilon n^2\le|M(c_0)|<\frac{n^2}{2k},\)

so \(\varepsilon<\frac{1}{2k}\).

## 4 A reconstruction lemma

Our aim is to construct a _k_-coloring with relatively few monochromatic edges. We do this by coloring the vertices in several stages. When coloring a new stage, we only need to count monochromatic edges joining its vertices to vertices in the same stage or in earlier stages. The general strategy is therefore to color the vertices from easy to difficult: vertices with large palette degrees are harder to handle and are deferred to later stages. At a given stage, vertices deferred to later stages are temporarily ignored. This is reflected in the construction below by emptying the palettes of these "more difficult" vertices. To control the total number of monochromatic edges, we assign each vertex a time at which its color is easiest to handle. The running minimum _E<sub>t</sub>_ records these best available thresholds.

**Lemma 4.1.** _Let_ \(P^0\supseteq P^1\supseteq\cdots\supseteq P^T\) _be palette systems with P_<sup>0</sup>(_v_)=\[_k_\] _for every v. Suppose that for every_ \(1\le t\le T\) _and every_ \(v\in U(P^t)\) _there is a color_ \(i\in P^t(v)\) _such that_ \(d_i^{P^t}(v)\le D_t\)_, where_ \(D_t\in[0,n]\)_, and suppose_<tbc>

\(\sum_{t=1}^TD_t\le kn.\) (1)

<tbc>_Let_<tbc>

\(a_t:=|U(P^{t-1})\backslash U(P^t)|,B_t:=\sum_{s=1}^ta_s=n-|U(P^t)|.\)

<tbc>_If_<tbc>

\(B_t\le\alpha tn(1\le t\le T),\) (2)

<tbc>_then there is a map_ \(c:V(G)\rightarrow[k]\) _with_<tbc>

\(|M(c)|\le\left(\alpha(k+1)+\frac{k}{T}\right)n^2.\) (3)

<tbc>_Proof._ Let _r_ be the first index attaining \(min_{1\le t\le T}D_t\). Then \(D_r\le kn/T\) since \(\sum_{t=1}^TD_t\le kn\). Define

\(E_0:=n,E_t:=min_{1\le s\le t}D_s.\)

Thus \(E_0\ge E_1\ge\cdots\ge E_T\) and \(\sum_{t=1}^TE_t\le kn\).

Let \(1=r_1<r_2<\cdots<r_j=r\) be the record indices of the running minimum, so that \(r_{\ell+1}\) is the next strict decrease after \(r_\ell\). Then<tbc>

\(E_{t-1}=D_{r_\ell}\text{whenever}r_\ell<t\le r_{\ell+1}.\) (4)

If _r_=1, the list contains only _r_1=1 and the intermediate layers below are empty. Partition _V(G_) into \(V(G)\backslash U(P^{r_1}),U(P^{r_\ell})\backslash U(P^{r_{\ell+1}})(1\le\ellr_), assigning to each vertex a witness color of degree at most _Dr_. Since \(|U(P^r)|\le n\), counting all possible neighbors gives at most _nDr_ monochromatic edges inside this part. Next add the remaining layers in reverse order. For a vertex in \(U(P^{r_\ell})\backslash U(P^{r_{\ell+1}})\), use a witness color in \(P^{r_\ell}\) of degree at most \(D_{r_\ell}\). Every already colored vertex uses a color belonging to its palette at time \(r_\ell\), by nestedness. Hence this vertex creates at most \(D_{r_\ell}\) new monochromatic edges to previously colored vertices. Finally color _V(G_)\\_U(P_1) arbitrarily, charging at most _n_ edges per vertex. Using (4), the total number of monochromatic edges is at most \(nD_r+\sum_{t=1}^ra_tE_{t-1}.\) (5) With _B_0=0, summation by parts gives \(\sum_{t=1}^ra_tE_{t-1}=B_rE_{r-1}+\sum_{t=1}^{r-1}B_t(E_{t-1}-E_t)\)
\(\le\alpha n\left(rE_{r-1}+\sum_{t=1}^{r-1}t(E_{t-1}-E_t)\right)\)
\(=\alpha n\sum_{t=0}^{r-1}E_t\)
\(=\alpha n\left(E_0+\sum_{t=1}^{r-1}E_t\right)\)
\(\le\alpha n\left(n+kn\right)\)
\(\le\alpha(k+1)n^2.\) Together with \(nD_r\le kn^2/T\), we have reached the conclusion that there is a way to color the graph as required. ## 5 The trial coloring process The trial coloring process calculates palettes _Q_0_,P_1_,Q_1_,P_2_,Q_2_,..._ and chooses pivots _f_1_,...,fT_ using colors _i_1_,...,iT_. Two features of this process are crucial. First, it only removes colors from palettes and never adds any. Second, it is dynamic: each operation is based on the current palette system, rather than on the initial graph alone. Fix a total order on _V(G_) for tie-breaking. Given \(A\subseteq V(G)\) and prescribed colors \(i_1,i_2,\dots\in[k]\), the trial coloring process is defined as follows. **Trial coloring process.**
**Input:** A graph _G_=(_V,E_), an integer \(k\ge 1\), a set \(A\subseteq V\) , a round limit _T_, a prescribed color sequence \((i_t)_{t\ge 1}\), and a fixed total order on _V_ for tie-breaking.
**Output:** The pivots, thresholds, cap palettes, and palette systems generated before the process stops or completes _T_ rounds.

1. For every \(v\in V\) , set \(Q^0(v)\leftarrow[k]\); set \(P^0\leftarrow Q^0\) and \(F_0\leftarrow\varnothing\).<tbc>

2. **for** _t_=1,2_,...,T_ **do**<tbc>

3. If some \(v\in A\) has \(Q^{t-1}(v)=\varnothing\), or \(A\backslash F_{t-1}=\varnothing\), stop.<tbc>

4. Choose \(f_t\in A\backslash F_{t-1}\) maximizing _m_<sub>_Q_<sup>_t_-1</sup></sub>(_v_), breaking ties by the fixed order; set \(D_t\leftarrow m_{Q^{t-1}}(f_t)\).<tbc>

5. Form the cap palette _P<sup>t</sup>_ from _Q_<sup>_t_-1</sup> according to the rule below.<tbc>

6. If \(i_t\notin P^t(f_t)\), stop.<tbc>

7. Set \(F_t\leftarrow F_{t-1}\cup\{f_t\}\) and initially set \(Q^t(w)\leftarrow P^t(w)\) for every \(w\in V\) .<tbc>

8. Set \(Q^t(f_t)\leftarrow\{i_t\}\); for every \(u\in N_G(f_t)\), set \(Q^t(u)\leftarrow P^t(u)\backslash\{i_t\}\).<tbc>

9. **end for**<tbc>

10. **return** the generated pivots, thresholds, cap palettes, and palette systems.

<tbc>The cap update in step 5 is

\(P^t(w)=\left\{\begin{array}{ c c }
\varnothing, & Q^{t-1}(w)\neq\varnothing\text{and}m_{Q^{t-1}}(w)>D_t, \\
Q^{t-1}(w), & \text{otherwise.}
\end{array}\right.\)

In particular,

\(U(P^t)=\{w:Q^{t-1}(w)\neq\varnothing\text{and}m_{Q^{t-1}}(w)\le D_t\}.\) (6)

In step 5, all degrees and the threshold are computed from the palette system _Q_<sup>_t_-1</sup> before any cap or neighbor update.

## 6 Analysis of the trial coloring process

### 6.1 Process invariants

**Lemma 6.1.** _For every completed run:_

1. \(P^0\supseteq P^1\supseteq\cdots\) _, and every_ \(v\in U(P^t)\) _has a color_ \(i\in P^t(v)\) _with_ \(d_i^{P^t}(v)\le D_t\)_; moreover_ \(0\le D_t\le n\).<tbc>

_2._ _On every run completing T rounds,_<tbc>

\(\sum_{t=1}^TD_t\le kn.\) \(\text{(7)}\)

_3. If G_\[_A_\] _has a proper coloring_ \(\varphi:A\rightarrow[k]\)_, then, whenever round t is reached, the prescribed choice_ \(i_t=\varphi(f_t)\) _is legal. If_ \(|A|\ge T\)_, it completes T rounds and preserves_ \(\varphi(v)\) _in the palette of every_ \(v\in A\) _throughout; in particular_ \(A\subseteq U(P^t)\) _for all_ \(t\le T\).<tbc>

<tbc>_Proof._ For the first assertion, caps only empty entire palettes and never add labels. If \(v\in U(P^t)\), then \(m_{Q^{t-1}}(v)\le D_t\) by (6). Choose \(i^*\in Q^{t-1}(v)\) attaining this minimum. Since _v_ was not emptied, _P<sup>t</sup>(v_)=_Q_<sup>_t_-1</sup>(_v_), and hence

\(d_{i^*}^{P^t}(v)\le d_{i^*}^{Q^{t-1}}(v)=m_{Q^{t-1}}(v)\le D_t.\)

The bounds on _D<sub>t</sub>_ are immediate from its definition and \(|N_G(f_t)|\le n-1\).

For the second assertion, since \(i_t\in Q^{t-1}(f_t)\),<tbc>

\(d_{i_t}^{Q^{t-1}}(f_t)\ge D_t.\)

<tbc>Choose _D<sub>t</sub>_ distinct neighbors _u_<sub>1</sub>_,...,u<sub>D<sub>t</sub></sub>_ carrying color _i<sub>t</sub>_ in their palettes. At the end of the round, each such vertex has lost the label _i<sub>t</sub>_: it is either emptied by the cap or loses _i<sub>t</sub>_ in the neighbor update. Therefore

\(\lambda(Q^{t-1})-\lambda(Q^t)\ge D_t.\)

Summing over rounds and telescoping yields (7), since \(\lambda(Q^0)=kn\).

For the third assertion, let \(\varphi\) be a proper coloring of _G_\[_A_\]. We prove inductively that, after each round, \(\varphi(v)\) remains in the palette of every \(v\in A\); moreover, each selected pivot _f<sub>s</sub>_ has the singleton palette \(\{\varphi(f_s)\}\), and no neighbor of _f<sub>s</sub>_ carries \(\varphi(f_s)\) in its palette. These assertions hold initially, with the pivot assertions vacuous.

Suppose they hold before round _t_. Every vertex of _A_ is active. If \(|A|\ge T\) and \(t\le T\), then an unchosen vertex remains, so _f<sub>t</sub>_ is defined. Every unchosen \(v\in A\) is a candidate in the maximization defining _f<sub>t</sub>_, and consequently<tbc>

\(m_{Q^{t-1}}(v)\le m_{Q^{t-1}}(f_t)=D_t.\)

<tbc>Thus the cap does not empty its palette and preserves \(\varphi(v)\). For an earlier pivot _f<sub>s</sub>_, the inductive assertions give

\(d_{\varphi(f_s)}^{Q^{t-1}}(f_s)=0,\)

so its singleton palette is also preserved by the cap. In particular, \(\varphi(f_t)\in P^t(f_t)\), making the prescribed color choice legal.

The update deletes \(\varphi(f_t)\) only from neighbors of _f<sub>t</sub>_. Properness of \(\varphi\) ensures that no such neighbor in _A_ loses its prescribed color. The pivot _f<sub>t</sub>_ receives the singleton palette \(\{\varphi(f_t)\}\), and all its neighbors lose that color. The assertions for earlier pivots remain valid. This completes the induction and proves that the run completes _T_ rounds.

## 6.2 The missing-cap lemma

**Lemma 6.2.** _Suppose that G is_ \(\varepsilon\)_-far from being k-colorable. Let_<tbc>

\(T:=\left\lceil\frac{4k}{\varepsilon}\right\rceil\ge 1,\alpha:=\frac{\varepsilon}{4(k+1)}.\)

<tbc>_Every run completing T rounds has some_ \(1\le t\le T\) _with_

\(|U(P^t)|\le(1-\alpha t)n.\) (8)

_Consequently, if_ \(|A|\ge T\) _and G_\[_A_\] _is k-colorable, then the proper-coloring run contains all of A in the cap at that time._

_Proof._ By Lemma 3.2, whenever a relevant graph exists we have \(0<\varepsilon<1/(2k)\). Hence

\(\alpha T\le\frac{4k+\varepsilon}{4(k+1)}<1,\)

so all right-hand sides in (8) are positive.

Assume for contradiction that (8) fails for every _t_. Then<tbc>

\(B_t=n-|U(P^t)|<\alpha tn,\)

<tbc>so \(B_t\le\alpha tn\). Lemma 6.1 supplies all the other hypotheses of Lemma 4.1, including (7). Therefore some coloring _c_ satisfies

\(|M(c)|\le\left(\alpha(k+1)+\frac{k}{T}\right)n^2\le\frac{\varepsilon}{2}n^2<\varepsilon n^2,\)

contradicting Lemma 3.1. The final statement follows from the last part of Lemma 6.1.

### 6.3 Deletion stability

**Lemma 6.3.** _Suppose that a run executed on A has first t pivots f_<sub>1</sub>_,...,f<sub>t</sub>. If_

\(\{f_1,\dots,f_t\}\subseteq A'\subseteq A,\)

_then running on_ \(A'\) _with the same successive color choices produces the same first t pivots, thresholds, caps, and palette updates._

_Proof._ The main idea is that the choices of pivots and the cap palettes do not change. Induct on the rounds. The initial palettes are independent of the sample set. If the first _s_-1 rounds agree, the current palettes agree pointwise. The original pivot _f<sub>s</sub>_ remains a candidate in \(A'\), and every other candidate in \(A'\) was also a candidate in _A_. Thus its maximality and the fixed tie-breaking order are unchanged. The cap and update depend only on the current palettes, the pivot, and the chosen color. Since the original run completed _t_ rounds, the same pointwise equality also prevents the restricted run from stopping earlier.

## 7 Sampling upper bound

The container viewpoint makes the counting strategy explicit. For each _k_-colorable induced subgraph on _q_ vertices, the process selects pivots and their colors, which determine the relevant palette container when replayed on a suitable subset of the sample. The counting proof supplements this pivot fingerprint with a block choice and the ordered vertices in the selected blocks; this replay seed contains all pivots and, by deletion stability, reproduces the same container as the full-sample run. The remaining sample positions must lie inside that container. We count these descriptions and bound the probability of such a completion, then take a union bound over the descriptions.

For each \(t\in\{1,2,\dots,T\}\), partition the positions \[_q_\] deterministically into 2_t_ nonempty blocks whose sizes differ by at most one.

Our counting argument encodes each colorable sample by one of a small number of _descriptions_. We first record what such a description is.

**Definition 7.1** (Description)**.** A _description_ is a tuple

\((t,W,\mathbf{i},u_1,\dots,u_a,v_1,\dots,v_b)\) (9)

consisting of the following data:

1. an integer \(t\in\{1,\dots,T\}\);<tbc>

2. a _t_-element set \(W\subseteq[2t]\) of block indices of the deterministic partition of \[_q_\] into 2_t_ blocks used in the construction of _A_<sub>0</sub>;<tbc>

3. a color string \(\mathbf{i}=(i_1,\dots,i_t)\in[k]^t\);<tbc>

4. an ordered tuple (_u_<sub>1</sub>_,...,u<sub>a</sub>_) of distinct vertices of _G_, with _a_ equal to the total size of the blocks in _W_;<tbc>

5. an ordered tuple (_v_<sub>1</sub>_,...,v<sub>b</sub>_) of distinct vertices of _G_, with _b=q-a_.

The tuple is _retained_ if _u_<sub>1</sub>_,...,u<sub>a</sub>,v_<sub>1</sub>_,...,v<sub>b</sub>_ are pairwise distinct and, on replaying the process from _A_<sub>0</sub>:={_u_<sub>1</sub>_,...,u<sub>a</sub>_} with the color string **i**, the process completes _t_ rounds and its true cap _C_:=_U(P<sup>t</sup>_) satisfies<tbc>

\(\{u_1,\dots,u_a,v_1,\dots,v_b\}\subseteq C,|V(G)\backslash C|\ge\alpha tn.\) (10)

For a retained description we write

\(h:=|V(G)\backslash C|.\) (11)

We now show in Proposition 7.2 that every colorable sample _S_ gives rise to at least one retained description, and that each retained description determines at most one sample. There are then only few possible descriptions, and each one is realized by a _q_-tuple with exponentially small probability.

**Proposition 7.2.** _With T and_ \(\alpha\) _as above, let_

\(q:=max\left\{4T,\left\lceil\frac{4}{\alpha}log(16k)\right\rceil\right\}.\) (12)

_For every_ \(\varepsilon\)_-far graph G, a uniformly random q-vertex induced subgraph is non-k-colorable with probability at least_ 2/3_. Consequently,_

\(S_k(\varepsilon)=O\big(\frac{klogk}{\varepsilon}\big).\) (13)

_Proof._ If _n\<q_, we sample all vertices. Since \(\varepsilon n^2>0\), an \(\varepsilon\)-far graph cannot itself be _k_-colorable, so the success probability is one.

**Get a retained description from a** _k_**-colorable** _S_

Assume \(n\ge q\), and equivalently sample a uniformly random ordered tuple _S_=(_x_<sub>1</sub>_,...,x<sub>q</sub>_) of distinct vertices. Suppose _G_\[_S_\] is _k_-colorable and fix a proper coloring \(\varphi:S\rightarrow[k]\). Run the trial coloring process with _A=S_ and choose \(i_t=\varphi(f_t)\). By Lemma 6.1, since \(|S|\ge 4T\ge T\), the run completes _T_ rounds and preserves _S_ in every cap. Lemma 6.2 gives some \(1\le t\le T\) and _C_<sup>∗</sup>=_U(P<sup>t</sup>_) such that

\(S\subseteq C^*,|V(G)\backslash C^*|\ge\alpha tn.\) (14)

The _t_ pivots occupy at most _t_ blocks. Choose a _t_-subset \(W\subseteq[2t]\) containing those blocks, adding arbitrary blocks if necessary. Let _A_<sub>0</sub> be the sample vertices in the blocks indexed by _W_, and put _B_<sub>0</sub>=_S_\\_A_<sub>0</sub>. Write

\(a:=|A_0|,b:=|B_0|=q-a.\)

Then \(\{f_1,\dots,f_t\}\subseteq A_0\subseteq S\). By Lemma 6.3, replaying the first _t_ rounds from _A_<sub>0</sub> with the same color string \(\mathbf{i}=(\varphi(f_1),\dots,\varphi(f_t))\) produces the same cap _C_<sup>∗</sup>. The ordered _u_-part (_u_<sub>1</sub>_,...,u<sub>a</sub>_) corresponding to _S_ is obtained from _A_<sub>0</sub> by listing its vertices in increasing order of their sample positions (their relative position is the same as in the ordered tuple _S_), and _v_<sub>1</sub>_,...,v<sub>b</sub>_ are obtained in the same way from _B_<sub>0</sub>. Once _t_ and _W_ are fixed, the correspondence between the ordered _q_-tuples _S_ and (_u_<sub>1</sub>_,...,u<sub>a</sub>,v_<sub>1</sub>_,...,v<sub>b</sub>_) is a bijection.

Consequently,

\((t,W,(\varphi(f_1),\dots,\varphi(f_t)),u_1,\dots,u_a,v_1,\dots,v_b)\)

is a retained description in the sense of Definition 7.1: the replay from _A_<sub>0</sub> with the color string **i** yields the cap _C_<sup>∗</sup>, and (14) gives both \(S\subseteq C^*\) and \(|V(G)\backslash C^*|\ge\alpha tn\). Hence every colorable sample _S_ admits at least one retained description (there may be multiple possible choices of _t_, _W_, \(\varphi\)).

**Recover** _S_ **from the retained description**

Conversely, the sample _S_ itself is recovered from a retained description as follows: by _W_ and the block partition we know which of the _q_ sample positions belong to the _u_-part and which to the _v_-part, the two tuples are listed in increasing order of their positions, and the vertices of the two tuples are pairwise distinct. Hence a retained description determines at most one ordered sample.

**Counting the number of retained descriptions.**

The ordered _v_-part of a retained description must consist of distinct vertices of _C_\\_A_<sub>0</sub>: in the _v_-positions of the sample we have placed vertices that avoid the true missing set _V(G_)\\_C_, and no vertex may appear in both the _u_-part and the _v_-part. Since \(A_0\subseteq C\), there are exactly _n-a-h_ available vertices, and hence at most \(P_{n-a-h}^b\) choices for the ordered _v_-part.

For fixed _t,W,_**i**, the block-size estimate gives

\(a\le t\left\lceil\frac{q}{2t}\right\rceil\le\frac{q}{2}+t,b=q-a\ge\frac{q}{2}-t\ge\frac{q}{4},\) (15)

where \(q\ge 4T\ge 4t\). We first give a common upper bound. For fixed _t,W,_**i**, the numbers _a_ and _b_ are fixed, but the replayed cap and its missing-set size may depend on the ordered _u_-tuple. Let U_<sub>t,W,_**i**</sub> be the set of ordered tuples **u**=(_u_<sub>1</sub>_,...,u<sub>a</sub>_) of distinct vertices for which replaying the process on _A_<sub>0</sub>={_u_<sub>1</sub>_,...,u<sub>a</sub>_} with color string **i** completes _t_ rounds and yields a cap _C=U(P<sup>t</sup>_) satisfying \(A_0\subseteq C\) and \(|V(G)\backslash C|\ge\alpha tn\). For \(\mathbf{u}\in\mathcal{U}_{t,W,\mathbf{i}}\), write _h_(**u**):=|_V(G_)\\_C_| for the missing-set size of its replayed cap.

Conditioned on a particular ordered _u_-tuple, the remaining positions are filled uniformly by an ordered _b_-tuple from _V(G_)\\_A_<sub>0</sub>. Thus, writing _h=h_(**u**) temporarily, the fraction of these completions that avoid the missing set is

\(\frac{P_{n-a-h}^b}{P_{n-a}^b}=\prod_{j=0}^{b-1}\frac{n-a-h-j}{n-a-j}=\prod_{j=0}^{b-1}\left(1-\frac{h}{n-a-j}\right)\le\left(1-\frac{h}{n-a}\right)^b\le exp\left(-\frac{hb}{n-a}\right)\le exp\left(-\frac{hb}{n}\right)\le e^{-\alpha tb}\le e^{-\alpha tq/4}.\text{(16)}\)

The displayed product is used only when \(b\le n-a-h\); otherwise the fraction is zero and the same bound holds. The condition \(A_0\subseteq C\) ensures that the entire missing set lies in _V(G_)\\_A_<sub>0</sub>. The penultimate inequality uses \(h\ge\alpha tn\) and \(n-a\le n\).

For fixed _t,W,_**i**, let _N_<sub>_t,W,_**i**</sub> denote the number of retained descriptions. Summing separately over the ordered _u_-tuples, rather than treating _h_ as a constant, gives

\(\frac{N_{t,W,\mathbf{i}}}{P_n^q}=\frac{1}{P_n^a}\sum_{\mathbf{u}\in\mathcal{U}_{t,W,\mathbf{i}}}\frac{P_{n-a-h(\mathbf{u})}^b}{P_{n-a}^b}\le\frac{|\mathcal{U}_{t,W,\mathbf{i}}|}{P_n^a}e^{-\alpha tq/4}\le e^{-\alpha tq/4}.\)

Here we used \(P_n^q=P_n^aP_{n-a}^b\) and \(|\mathcal{U}_{t,W,\mathbf{i}}|\le P_n^a\).

There are at most \(\genfrac(){pt}{2}{2t}{t}\le 4^t\) choices for _W_ and _k<sup>t</sup>_ choices for the color string. Every colorable sample yields at least one retained description, even though its proper coloring may depend on the<tbc>

sample. Summing the preceding bound over all strings and block choices therefore gives, by (12), \(Pr[G[S]\text{is}k\text{-colorable}]\le\sum_{t=1}^T(4k)^te^{-\alpha tq/4}\)
\(\le\sum_{t=1}^T(4k)^t(16k)^{-t}\)
\(=\sum_{t=1}^T4^{-t}\le\frac{1}{3}.\) Thus the induced subgraph is non-_k_-colorable with probability at least 2/3. Finally, \(T=O(k/\varepsilon)\), \(\frac{1}{\alpha}=\frac{4(k+1)}{\varepsilon}\) , and log(16_k_)=_O_(log_k_), proving (13). ## 8 Concluding remarks The proof combines the container method with a palette-based coloring process tailored to _k_- colorability. The reason we can improve upon the bound of [7, 19] is that our method allows us to introduce a structure to choose _t_ blocks out of 2_t_ blocks. By contrast, the fingerprint in [7, 19] is effectively enumerated by a factor of the form \(\genfrac(){pt}{2}{q}{t}\), together with the corresponding color assignments. Without nontrivial modifications, their mechanism does not support a \(\genfrac(){pt}{2}{2t}{t}\)-type encoding like the one used in our algorithm. In the Kushnir-Shapira construction, the container at round _t_ does not depend on the entire independent set _I_; it depends only on the fingerprint from the first _t_ rounds. However, every vertex in vert(_Ft_) must be assigned a color in order to determine _Ft_. If one instead starts with a subset \(V\subseteq\text{vert}(I)\) without specifying the colors of all vertices in _V_ , different choices of colors can lead to different processes and hence to different projected containers vert(_Ct_). See Appendix A for a concrete example illustrating the algorithms. A second important ingredient is how the assumption that the original graph is \(\varepsilon\)-far from _k_-colorable forces some properties. Intuitively, call a vertex "bad" at a given stage if the process is unwilling to assign it a color. If the sampled subgraph is _k_-colorable, the process can preserve its proper coloring and continue; conversely, if too few vertices become bad throughout the process, the reconstruction lemma produces a coloring of the original graph with fewer than \(\varepsilon n^2\) monochromatic edges, contradicting \(\varepsilon\)-farness. Moreover, a coloring process in which many such "bad" vertices appear occurs with very low probability if the subgraph _S_ is _k_-colorable. ## Statement on AI usage The author had early discussions with ChatGPT about how to approach the palette system.
